source: Hand-researched by the site author from primary sources; last verified August 2026
disclaimer: Plain-English summaries for orientation — not legal advice.

cells.key_law: No single space act — a patchwork: 51 U.S.C. ch. 509 (launch & reentry), the Communications Act (spectrum), 51 U.S.C. ch. 601 (remote sensing), and the Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015.
cells.licensing: Split by activity: FAA licenses launch and reentry, FCC licenses spectrum, NOAA licenses remote sensing. Novel in-space activities still have no assigned licenser — an August 2025 executive order tasked Commerce with proposing a mission-authorization process, now before Congress.
cells.liability: Launch operators must insure up to a government-calculated "maximum probable loss"; above that, the government promises to cover third-party claims up to a cap in the low billions — a bargain designed to make launch insurable.
cells.registration: The State Department keeps the U.S. registry of space objects under the UN Registration Convention.
cells.resources: First mover: the 2015 law grants U.S. citizens ownership of space resources they obtain, while explicitly claiming no sovereignty over celestial bodies.
cells.distinctive: The world's largest space economy runs on launch-era statutes — the "mission authorization gap" for stations, servicing, and mining is the live debate this site tracks.

sources.label: FAA Office of Commercial Space Transportation

cells.key_law: Law of 20 July 2017 on the exploration and use of space resources + Law of 15 December 2020 on space activities.
cells.licensing: Government ministers authorize and continuously supervise each mission individually; the 2020 law extends licensing to all space activities, not just resource ventures.
cells.liability: Operators bear liability and must demonstrate financial soundness and insurance to be authorized; the state can recover what it pays out on international claims.
cells.registration: A national registry of space objects maintained under the 2020 law.
cells.resources: Second country on Earth (2017) to declare that space resources are "capable of being appropriated" — the legal cornerstone of its bid to host the space-mining industry.
cells.distinctive: A country of under 700,000 people deliberately wrote itself into the center of commercial space law — legislation as industrial policy.

cells.key_law: Space Activities Act (2016) + Space Resources Act (2021).
cells.licensing: The Cabinet Office licenses each launch vehicle, launch site, and satellite-control operation under the 2016 Act.
cells.liability: Liability for launch damage is channeled exclusively to the launch operator, who must carry insurance — with government compensation above it. Customers and manufacturers are shielded by design.
cells.registration: National registration is handled through the Cabinet Office licensing system.
cells.resources: The 2021 Act grants ownership of extracted space resources to operators holding an approved business plan — permits are published publicly.
cells.distinctive: "Channeling" all launch liability to one party is a deliberate pro-business design — a satellite customer in Japan knows exactly what risk they do and don't carry.

cells.key_law: Federal Law No. 12 of 2019 on the Regulation of the Space Sector.
cells.licensing: The UAE Space Agency licenses a deliberately broad range of activities — launch, satellite operation, human spaceflight, and space resource activities are all named in the statute.
cells.liability: Operators must carry insurance at levels set by the Space Agency; the state can recover payments it makes under international liability claims.
cells.registration: The Space Agency maintains the national registry of space objects.
cells.resources: The 2019 law explicitly contemplates permits for the exploration, extraction, and use of space resources — among the first statutes drafted with mining already in mind.
cells.distinctive: One modern statute written in a single stroke (2019) — covering debris mitigation, human spaceflight, and mining before most countries had addressed any of them.

cells.key_law: Space Industry Act 2018 + Space Industry Regulations 2021.
cells.licensing: The Civil Aviation Authority licenses launches, spaceports, and orbital operations conducted from the UK.
cells.liability: Each license carries a liability limit set by the regulator, with mandatory insurance up to it — operators aren't exposed to unlimited claims; the state takes the tail risk.
cells.registration: The UK keeps its own registry of launches and orbital objects alongside its UN registration.
cells.resources: No space-resources legislation — the UK has not followed the US, Luxembourg, Japan, and UAE down the ownership route.
cells.distinctive: The first European country to license an orbital launch attempt from home soil (Cornwall, 2023) — a real-world stress test of the whole framework.

cells.key_law: No statute yet — the Indian Space Policy 2023 plus IN-SPACe's Norms, Guidelines and Procedures (2024); a comprehensive Space Activities Bill has been in draft for years.
cells.licensing: IN-SPACe, a single-window regulator created in 2020, authorizes private space activities under policy rather than legislation — a bridge until Parliament acts.
cells.liability: No dedicated liability statute; authorization conditions and general law fill the gap — one of the strongest arguments made for passing the pending bill.
cells.registration: Registration is handled through IN-SPACe and Department of Space processes.
cells.resources: Policy language permits private resource recovery consistent with international law, but there is no statutory ownership grant yet.
cells.distinctive: A top-tier spacefaring nation running a private-sector space boom on policy documents rather than law — the world's most consequential "statute to come."
